So the "squashed" look in your screenshot must be something else. Two possibilities:

The screenshot is rendered at the WordPress editor preview width (not the public page), which often previews at a narrow column
The site's outer theme container is limiting it (parent constraint, not the .nlp3d rule)
Let me check the theme's article/main container:

Ran
Check parent containers constraining the .nlp3d width
FOUND IT FOR REAL THIS TIME. Rule [1]:

.is-layout-constrained > :where(:not(.alignleft):not(.alignright):not(.alignfull))
{ max-width: var(--wp--style--global--content-size) }
This is a WordPress core block-theme rule. The parent <div class="entry-content alignfull wp-block-post-content has-global-padding is-layout-constrained ..."> has is-layout-constrained. Every direct child that is NOT .alignleft / .alignright / .alignfull gets capped at var(--wp--style--global--content-size) — which the theme defines (usually 800–1200px, sometimes 380–600px on narrow block themes).

The .nlp3d block isn't getting .alignfull or .alignwide on it, so the theme's content-size cap squashes it BEFORE the plugin's width:min(1420px, ...) rule can even fight back. The plugin's !important doesn't help because the cap is on the parent's children selector, which the plugin's selector doesn't match (.entry-content > .nlp3d ≠ .is-layout-constrained > :where(...)). They're applying to the same element but the CSS specificity puzzle isn't being won by the plugin reliably across all themes.

The fix (real this time)
Add alignfull to the .nlp3d wrapper when it's emitted into a block-theme entry-content. That makes it skip the :where(:not(.alignfull)) c

Continuing the technical-SEO work. Highest-impact items I can do safely via REST: verify the http/https canonical situation (I saw http:// in the sitemap earlier — that's a real ranking risk), check indexability, and add breadcrumbs. Investigating first before changing anything.

Diagnosed http/https canonical, robots, breadcrumbs, indexability
Excellent news — the technical baseline is better than I feared:

✅ Canonicals are https (Yoast outputs correct https canonicals)
✅ robots meta: index, follow — fully indexable
✅ BreadcrumbList schema already present (Yoast emits it)
✅ og:url https
The only real inconsistency: siteurl is http:// while home is https:// — which is why the sitemap lists http URLs. That's a genuine (minor) technical-SEO fix. Let me check the navigation menu and Yoast schema, and fix the siteurl safely.

Checked navigation block, Yoast schema types, site representation
Schema check reveals a real gap: the lawyer page emits WebPage + Organization but no Article or Person/Attorney schema — that's the E-E-A-T signal we want for legal pages (and a reason the strategy flagged spokes should eventually be Posts, not Pages).

On siteurl: I'm deliberately not flipping it. home, canonicals, and og:url are all already https — Google sees https. Flipping siteurl on a managed host (UPress, edge SSL termination) risks an admin redirect-loop for marginal benefit. Not worth the risk for a tired owner. Documenting as an optional UPress-panel fix.

Let me check the navigation menu content — site-wide nav links are high-value internal linking.

Read navigation block raw content
The navigation is just <!-- wp:page-list /--> — which dumps all 42 flat pages into an unprioritized, unwieldy menu. That's poor for both UX and SEO (no hierarchy signal, link equity diluted across 42 equal nav links). I'll replace it with a curated, pillar-first navigation with logical submenus — exactly the hierarchy you asked for. Site-wide nav links to pillars
